To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the 5'UTR of the c-myc gene is a potent repressor of its own translation; 2) c-myc 5'UTRs contain a novel RNA secondary structure that is essential for its inhibitory function; 3) c-myc translation is regulated by a balance between the repressive and stimulatory activities of its 5'UTr and the 3'UTR; 4) the 3' untranslated region of the p21
5' and/or 3' UTrs can affect the rate of translation of proto-oncogene and tumour suppressors and can contribute to tumorigenesis.
the 5' UTRs of proto-oncogene and tumour suppressors are involved in the regulation of the rate of protein synthesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of gene expression at the level of translation initiation and how aberrant control of this process may contribute to cancer development.
the aberrant regulation of translation and how this may lead to the development of tumour cells.
the role of RNA structure and RNA-protein interactions in the regulation of gene expression and how changes in this control can lead to tumorigenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rate of translation is a key factor in the control of protein synthesis and that changes in this rate can contribute to the development of cancer.
the rate of translation is a key regulatory mechanism for gene expression and that the 5' and the 3' UTRS are key players in the regulation of the rate of translation.
there is a clear link between aberrant regulation of translation of proto-oncogene and tumour suppressors and cancer development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
translation initiation plays an important role in tumorigeness.
the 5'- and 3'-untranslated regions of proto-oncogene and tumour suppressors play an important role in the regulation and expression of these genes.
the aberrant regulation of translation of specific genes, through changes in the 5' UTR, can contribute to the development and maintenance of the malignant phenotype.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the aberrant regulation of translation can play a key role not only in tumorigenensis but also in the development of chemoresistance.
the rate of translation of specific genes can be altered by the presence of RNA secondary structure in the 5' and/or 3' UTrs of the corresponding mRNAs.
the regulation of translation is a key component of the control of geneexpression.
